title: Power of a Number
directAnswer: Use binary exponentiation: while `n > 0`, if `n` is odd multiply the answer by `x`, then square `x` and halve `n`. O(log n).

rules: Odd bit → multiply; always square base, shift n.
remember.takeaway: Square-and-multiply turns power, modpow, and matrix power into log time.
remember.formula: res=1; while n>0: if n&1: res*=x; x*=x; n>>=1
antiSignals: n tiny — a plain loop is fine and clearer

problemStatement: Given a base `x` and a non-negative exponent `n`, compute `xⁿ` (assume the result fits in a 64-bit integer).
understanding: Fast exponentiation: square the base and halve the exponent, multiplying into the result on odd bits — O(log n) instead of O(n).

approaches.name: Fast (binary) exponentiation
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Binary (fast) exponentiation computes xⁿ in O(log n) multiplications instead of the O(n) of a naive loop, by exploiting the binary representation of the exponent.

**The core idea.** Repeatedly squaring the base produces x¹, x², x⁴, x⁸, … — the powers of x at each bit position. Write n in binary; xⁿ is the product of exactly those squared powers where n has a 1-bit. So scan n bit by bit: if the current bit is 1, multiply it into the result; either way, square the base and shift n right.

**Why this is log n.** Each step halves n (`n >>= 1`), so there are about log₂(n) iterations, each doing a constant number of multiplications. For n = 1,000,000 that's ~20 multiplies versus a million.

**The base case.** x⁰ = 1, handled because the loop runs zero times and the result starts at 1. A simple O(n) loop is acceptable for small n, but showing the O(log n) trick is the distinguishing move.
hints: A loop multiplying x n times is O(n). Can you use the binary form of n?
Squaring gives x, x², x⁴, x⁸… — multiply in the ones matching n's 1-bits.
If n is odd, fold x into the result; then square x and halve n.
approaches.insight: A simple O(n) loop is acceptable, but showing the O(log n) trick is what distinguishes a strong answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: the exponent halves each iteration, so ~log₂(n) iterations with O(1) work each.

java.explanation: Multiply in the current power of x when this exponent bit is set.
Move to the next squared base and next exponent bit.

dryRun.intro: Square the base; multiply in on 1-bits.

edgeCases.behavior: Five-ish steps give 1024 with far fewer multiplies than 10.

pitfalls: Using an O(n) loop when O(log n) is expected.
Forgetting x⁰ = 1, or not squaring x every iteration.

commonMistakes: Writing an O(n) loop when O(log n) is expected.

patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Binary exponentiation. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know binary exponentiation and can connect it to the exponent's bits.

interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Generalise to modular exponentiation (`% mod` each multiply) used in hashing/crypto.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the exponent non-negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll assume n ≥ 0; negative n means 1/xⁿ (a double result).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need it modulo something?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If so, take the modulus after each multiply — modular exponentiation.
